title: Static-Dynamic Disentanglement for Efficient Multi-Frame Vision-Language-Action Models
claim: Prior models re-encode every frame, exceeding context and recomputing; separating static from dynamic tokens enables multi-frame context and cache reuse.
layout: 2 stacked rows (prior/ours), each with two timesteps joined by Next Step arrow
description: The figure has two horizontal bands separated by a black line: 'Existing VLAs' on top and 'Ours' below. Each band shows two rounded KV-cache boxes, one per timestep, joined by a large 'Next Step' arrow. In the top band, grids of yellow and red cells fill the cache. The red cells carry the note 'exceeds context budgets!'. Image Token boxes feed upward into them. Red crosses mark 'Multi-frame Integration' and 'Efficient Inference' as failures. In the bottom band, one large blue static grid sits beside thin yellow dynamic columns labeled t to t+3. In the next step the blue grid is marked 'Cached', with a 'skip' arrow crossed out, and the dynamic columns shift to t+1 through t+4. Green check marks and green text mark both goals as achieved. The eye goes first to the red-versus-green labels.
caption: Our model solves two main challenges in existing VLAs with the proposed static-dynamic disentanglement. 1) By keeping one copy of static tokens across all timesteps, our model is able to squash observations of multiple steps to the model's context; 2) By moving static tokens in front of all dynamic tokens, our model could reuse the KV-cache of previous timesteps during rollouts.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for generalist robotic control. Built upon vision–language model (VLM) architectures, VLAs predict actions conditioned on visual observations and language instructions, achieving strong performance and generalization across tasks. However, VLAs face two major challenges: a limited context window for input frames and inefficient inference due to the quadratic attention complexity and large parameter counts. To this end, we propose Dysta, a framework that disentangles visual inputs into multi-level static and dynamic tokens, which enables (1) retaining a single copy of static tokens across frames to significantly reduce context length, and (2) reusing the key–value (KV) cache of static tokens through a lightweight recache gate that updates only when necessary. This design enables efficient multi-frame integration and efficient inference. In addition, we introduce a new benchmark that more effectively evaluates the multi-frame integration ability of VLAs. Experiments show that DySta improves multi-frame integration by 24.5\% across metrics on our benchmark and 23.3\% in absolute success rate on real-world memory-dependent tasks, while accelerating inference by 2.0× (with +2.3\% success rate) on simulation benchmarks and 2.2× (with +10.6\% success rate) on real-world general tasks.
